beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: RAG and EPR asks why individually relevant sources can form a weak evidence set.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its first half builds a practical understanding of retrieval and grounded generation.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The second develops Evidence Portfolio Retrieval as a testable research proposal.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The proposed change is to select complementary evidence for a specific scientific decision.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers can compare that idea with modern retrieval methods before accepting its claimed value.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Several retrieved documents can be individually relevant while repeating almost the same evidence.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A less similar source might contain the counterexample that changes the decision.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: One example asks what already exists behind a proposed manuscript-review system.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Similarity remains useful, but it cannot describe every property of a useful evidence set.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That distinction motivates the proposed shift from isolated rankings toward portfolios.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: An evidence portfolio is selected for a stated task under an explicit budget.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its members may provide support, criticism, boundary conditions, or alternative explanations.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Coverage, source dependence, and unresolved gaps remain part of the assessment.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Modern retrieval already includes related methods, so the proposal needs strong comparative baselines.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book treats improved downstream decisions as a hypothesis to test, not an established advantage.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Begin with the engineering account of indexing, retrieval, context construction, and evaluation.
